analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for people injured by doctors, lawyers, and other professionals to win lawsuits nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House committees until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced state malpractice laws with one federal rulebook covering doctors, lawyers, accountants, engineers, and other professionals. It shortened the window to sue, raised the bar for proving a professional was negligent, cut damage awards by any insurance or government benefits the injured person already received, capped what plaintiffs' lawyers could charge, and made punitive damages — the penalties meant to punish reckless conduct — very hard to win. No committee ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Licensed professionals — physicians, attorneys, accountants, engineers, architects — and the companies that sell them liability insurance. Fewer lawsuits would be filed, fewer would succeed, and the ones that did would pay out less: awards would be reduced dollar-for-dollar by any health insurance, workers' compensation, or government benefits the injured person received, future damages over $100,000 could be paid in installments, and punitive damages would require proof of malicious, reckless conduct that was an extreme departure from professional standards [S2] [S3]. Professionals would also get a shield for peer-review records, which could not be used against them in court [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill says a professional is not liable unless the injured person proves the professional was negligent and that, at the time of service, knowledge of the danger and a practical way to prevent it already existed [S2] [S3].

A professional whose work followed precise government contract specifications would not be liable at all for resulting harm, with an agency's compliance determination treated as conclusive proof [S2] [S3].

Punitive damages would require clear and convincing evidence of malicious and reckless disregard for safety, could never be awarded for ordinary negligence, would be decided in a separate trial at the professional's request, and any amount above three times compensatory damages would go to the government rather than the injured person [S2] [S3].
Records of risk-management and peer-review programs would be inadmissible in court, keeping internal reviews of professional performance out of plaintiffs' hands [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People harmed by professional negligence — a surgical error, a lawyer's blunder, a faulty engineering design. Their claims would face a three-year deadline from when they discovered or should have discovered the harm, a higher burden of proof, awards reduced by their own insurance and government benefits, several liability that limits what each defendant owes, and caps on their lawyers' contingency fees (a third of the first $250,000, less above that), which could make it harder to find an attorney willing to take an expensive case [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The collateral-source rule would reduce an injured person's award by benefits they or their family paid for — health insurance, workers' compensation, government programs — meaning the professional whose negligence caused the harm pays less while the victim's own coverage absorbs the cost [S2] [S3].

Federal preemption would override stronger state protections: the bill supersedes any inconsistent state law while letting states keep only additional protections for professionals, so states with more generous remedies for injured people would lose them [S3].

Punitive damages would be nearly unavailable: barred for ordinary negligence, barred without a compensatory award, decided in a separate proceeding if the defendant asks, and capped so the injured person keeps at most three times compensatory damages — even for conduct that recklessly endangered safety [S2] [S3].

Shielding peer-review and risk-management records from evidence would keep the very documents that show a professional knew about a problem out of court, making it harder to prove the case the bill already makes harder to bring [S3].

Supporters' case — that uniform national standards would reduce unpredictability, encourage innovation, and lower the cost of liability disputes — came at the price of shifting the costs of professional mistakes from professionals and insurers onto injured people and the programs that cover them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal was predictability and lower liability costs for professionals, and a well-designed reform could plausibly reduce defensive costs. But the specific terms tilt heavily the other way: shorter filing deadlines, tougher proof requirements, reduced awards, capped attorney fees, and near-impossible punitive damages all land on people who were already harmed through no fault of their own. The collateral-source provision is the clearest example — it cuts the wrongdoer's bill by money the victim already has, which does not lower society's costs so much as move them. The peer-review secrecy provision compounds this by hiding internal evidence. On balance, this bill's benefits flow to a concentrated group while its costs are spread across the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees, then to two subcommittees, where it sat without any hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Ritter (R-PA) introduced the bill on November 21, 1989, and it was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees the same day [S1] [S5].
In early December 1989 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured people kept the state malpractice laws they would have lost, and no federal shield was created for professionals or their insurers.

for.name: Rep. Don Ritter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in November 1989, framing it as promoting predictability and innovation in professional liability [S1] [S3].

for.name: Physicians, lawyers, and other professionals facing liability costs
for.what_they_did: Professional and insurance interests pressed for federal liability limits during the 1980s malpractice-insurance premium crisis, which produced a wave of federal tort-reform proposals like this one.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of first referral, chaired by Rep. John Conyers (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S5].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Second referral committee, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to its Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness subcommittee; no further action was taken [S5].

against.name: Trial lawyers and consumer groups
against.what_they_did: Organized against federal tort-revision proposals of this era, arguing they would strip injured patients and consumers of state-law remedies; the bill drew no committee action and never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so its level of support across the full House is unknown [S4].

industries.note: Fewer viable claims, awards reduced by the victim's own insurance and government benefits, and difficult punitive damages all shrink claim payouts [S2] [S3]. Insurers' savings come directly out of what injured people recover.

The bill cuts their exposure to malpractice suits through proof requirements, a government-contract immunity, evidence shields for peer review, and a shortened filing deadline [S2] [S3]. The protections come at the expense of the patients and clients they injure.

A mandatory contingency-fee schedule (a third of the first $250,000, less above that) and personal liability for attorneys who file weak suits reduce the economics of representing injured clients [S2] [S3]. Their financial stake here runs alongside injured people's access to the courts.
